chapters.title: International Code of Signals (ICS) -- single-flag meanings

sections.title: Flag A (Alfa)
sections.text: Flag A (Alfa): "I have a diver down; keep well clear at slow speed." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code.

sections.title: Flag B (Bravo)
sections.text: Flag B (Bravo): "I am taking in or discharging or carrying dangerous goods." Originally used by the Royal Navy specifically for military explosives.

sections.title: Flag C (Charlie)
sections.text: Flag C (Charlie): "Affirmative." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code. November and Charlie together ("NC" / "no" and "yes") is used as a distress signal.

sections.title: Flag D (Delta)
sections.text: Flag D (Delta): "Keep clear of me; I am manoeuvring with difficulty." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code.

sections.title: Flag E (Echo)
sections.text: Flag E (Echo): "I am altering my course to starboard." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code.

sections.title: Flag F (Foxtrot)
sections.text: Flag F (Foxtrot): "I am disabled; communicate with me."

sections.title: Flag G (Golf)
sections.text: Flag G (Golf): "I require a pilot." By fishing vessels near fishing grounds, Golf instead means: "I am hauling nets."

sections.title: Flag H (Hotel)
sections.text: Flag H (Hotel): "I have a pilot on board." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code.

sections.title: Flag I (India)
sections.text: Flag I (India): "I am altering my course to port." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code.

sections.title: Flag J (Juliett)
sections.text: Flag J (Juliett): "I am on fire and have dangerous cargo on board: keep well clear of me." Or: "I am leaking dangerous cargo."

sections.title: Flag K (Kilo)
sections.text: Flag K (Kilo): "I wish to communicate with you." Can indicate the intended medium: semaphore by hand-flags or arms; loud hailer (megaphone); Morse signalling lamp; or sound signals.

sections.title: Flag L (Lima)
sections.text: Flag L (Lima): "Stop immediately."

sections.title: Flag M (Mike)
sections.text: Flag M (Mike): "My vessel is stopped and making no way through the water." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code.

sections.title: Flag N (November)
sections.text: Flag N (November): "Negative." November and Charlie together ("NC" / "no" and "yes") is used as a distress signal.

sections.title: Flag O (Oscar)
sections.text: Flag O (Oscar): "Man overboard." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code; often attached to the man-overboard pole on boats.

sections.title: Flag P (Papa, 'the Blue Peter')
sections.text: Flag P (Papa), the "Blue Peter". In harbour: all persons should report on board as the vessel is about to proceed to sea. At sea, it may be used by fishing vessels to mean: "My nets have come fast upon an obstruction."

sections.title: Flag Q (Quebec)
sections.text: Flag Q (Quebec): "My vessel is 'healthy' and I request free pratique."

sections.title: Flag R (Romeo)
sections.text: Flag R (Romeo) has no ICS meaning as a single flag today. Prior to 1969 it meant: "The way is off my ship; you may feel your way past me."

sections.title: Flag S (Sierra)
sections.text: Flag S (Sierra): "I am operating astern propulsion." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code.

sections.title: Flag T (Tango)
sections.text: Flag T (Tango): "Keep clear of me." Also signallable on a ship's whistle using Morse code. By fishing boats it instead means: "Keep clear of me; I am engaged in pair trawling."

sections.title: Flag U (Uniform)
sections.text: Flag U (Uniform): "You are running into danger."

sections.title: Flag V (Victor)
sections.text: Flag V (Victor): "I require assistance."

sections.title: Flag W (Whiskey)
sections.text: Flag W (Whiskey): "I require medical assistance."

sections.title: Flag X (Xray)
sections.text: Flag X (Xray): "Stop carrying out your intentions and watch for my signals."

sections.title: Flag Y (Yankee)
sections.text: Flag Y (Yankee): "I am dragging my anchor."

sections.title: Flag Z (Zulu)
sections.text: Flag Z (Zulu): "I require a tug." By fishing vessels near fishing grounds, Zulu instead means: "I am shooting nets."

sections.title: How flag hoists are used
sections.text: A series of flags can spell out a message letter by letter (like a NATO phonetic spelling), OR a single flag can carry one of the fixed standard meanings above. Substitute/repeater flags let a message with duplicate letters be signalled without needing multiple sets of the same flag. Numeral pennants (0-9) are used for bearings, dates, times, and other numeric complements alongside letter flags. A flag/light signal is exactly as subordinate to COLREG as a VHF call -- it may assist mutual understanding but never overrides the COLREG-required action.

parsing_notes: Hand-transcribed from the single-flag ('ICS meaning as single flag') column of Wikipedia's 'International maritime signal flags' article table, CC BY-SA 4.0, derived from the IMO International Code of Signals (2005 ed.). Not a full scrape -- only the factual flag-meaning content, reworded into standalone reference sections.

Numeral pennants, the substitute flags, and multi-flag hoist code words (the full ICS phrase tables) are NOT included -- out of scope for this pass, same open gap noted in design_vhf_communications.md Sec 10.
